title: IELTS Academic 模擬試卷 一（範例）
description: 系統內建的完整範例試卷：聽力 40 題、閱讀 40 題、寫作兩篇、口說三部分。可直接指派給學生試考。

sections.title: Section 1
sections.instructions: Questions 1–10. Listen to a telephone conversation between a woman and a member of staff at a sports centre, and answer Questions 1–10.
sections.transcript:
TOM: Good morning, Wellsford Community Sports Centre, Tom speaking. How can I help you?

RACHEL: Oh, hello. I've just moved into the area and I'd like to find out about becoming a member.

TOM: Of course. What I can do is take your details over the phone and start a membership form for you, and then you just come in, check it and sign it. Is that all right?

RACHEL: That would be great, thank you.

TOM: Lovely. So, can I take your name?

RACHEL: Yes, it's Rachel Bettany.

TOM: Rachel ... and how do you spell the surname?

RACHEL: It's B-E-T-T-A-N-Y. Everybody writes it with one T, but there are two in the middle.

TOM: B-E-T-T-A-N-Y. Got it. And your address?

RACHEL: It's 42 Pelham Street — oh, no, sorry, ignore that, 42 is my parents' house. Mine is 24 Pelham Street, Wellsford.

TOM: 24 Pelham Street. And Pelham is P-E-L-H-A-M?

RACHEL: That's right.

TOM: Right. Now, we run two kinds of membership. Full membership is £46 a month and you can come in whenever we're open. Then there's off-peak, which is cheaper — that's any time up to four o'clock in the afternoon from Monday to Friday, plus all day on Sundays.

RACHEL: And how much is that one?

TOM: £35.50 — sorry, that was last year's price. It's £31.50 a month now.

RACHEL: £31.50. Well, I work from home, so weekday afternoons are actually perfect for me. Are Saturdays included?

TOM: I'm afraid not. Saturdays count as peak all day.

RACHEL: That's fine. I'll go for the off-peak membership, then.

TOM: Off-peak it is. Now, what are you mainly hoping to use the centre for? It helps us send you the right timetable.

RACHEL: Well, I used to swim a lot at school and I'd like to get back into that at some point. But the main thing, really, is badminton. I played all the way through university and I've missed it terribly.

TOM: Badminton — I'll put that down as your main activity. I should mention, actually, that the main pool is closed at the moment. The whole thing is being re-tiled and it won't reopen until the 29th of this month. There was talk of making it longer while the work was going on, but the budget wouldn't stretch to it in the end. When it does reopen it'll be open to members and non-members, just as it was before.

RACHEL: No hurry — I wasn't going to swim straight away. And is there a badminton club?

TOM: There is — it meets on Saturday mornings, from nine until eleven.

RACHEL: Ah. The trouble is that's exactly when I take my daughter to her music lesson, and my husband's away most weekends, so there's nobody else to do it. Somebody told me the club's quite competitive, but that wouldn't bother me at all — it's purely the timing.

TOM: That's a shame. There's a much more casual session on Wednesday afternoons, so that might suit you better.

RACHEL: Wednesday afternoon — yes, I'll try that one.

TOM: Now, every new member gets one free introductory session. Most people book theirs with a fitness instructor, who'll take you round the gym and put a programme together for you. You can have it with a swimming coach instead, but with the pool closed and badminton being your thing, I'd suggest the instructor.

RACHEL: Yes, the fitness instructor makes far more sense.

TOM: I'll book you in, then. We run them on the first Monday of the month, at half past six in the evening.

RACHEL: The first Monday. Fine.

TOM: And when you come in, could you bring two things? A passport photo, for your membership card — we used to take the picture here but the camera's been broken for months — and something with your address on it, so a bank statement or a utility bill.

RACHEL: A passport photo and proof of address. Right, I've written that down. Oh — is there anywhere to leave my things?

TOM: There are free lockers in the changing rooms, but you have to empty them every time you leave. If you want a locker you can keep permanently, with your racket and your kit in it, that's an extra £15 a year. It was £50 until this April, so it's quite good value now.

RACHEL: I'll think about that one.

TOM: No problem at all. Last thing — and we ask everybody this, it helps with our funding application — how did you hear about us?

RACHEL: Well, I'd looked at your website before I rang, so I knew roughly what was here. And there was a leaflet through the door a fortnight ago, though I think I threw it out without reading it properly. But the reason I actually picked up the phone was my next-door neighbour. She's been coming here for years and she wouldn't stop going on about it.

TOM: Wonderful. I'll put you down as a personal recommendation, then. So that's everything — I'll have the form ready at reception for you.

RACHEL: Thank you very much. Goodbye.

sections.title: Section 2
sections.instructions: Questions 11–20. Listen to a volunteer warden welcoming a group of visitors to a nature reserve, and answer Questions 11–20.
sections.transcript:
FIONA: Good morning everyone, and welcome to Bramblewood Nature Reserve. My name's Fiona and I'm one of the volunteer wardens here. Before we set off round the lake, let me give you a few minutes of background, and then I'll explain where everything is, because the reserve is a good deal bigger than it looks and people do get lost.

Bramblewood is only about forty years old as a nature reserve, which surprises most visitors. The whole of this valley belonged to the Bramble family — that's where the name comes from, nothing to do with brambles — and it was farmland, mostly sheep, until the 1950s. Then the family sold up, and from 1956 right through until 1978 the site was a gravel quarry. The lake you're about to walk round isn't natural at all: it's the flooded pit the quarry left behind. The company went out of business, the pit filled with water, the birds moved in almost immediately, and by 1983 it had been declared a reserve.

People often ask me what has changed most here in recent years. Visitor numbers are up — about ten per cent over five years, which is steady rather than dramatic. We've planted new woodland as well, but if I'm honest that's only two hectares up on the hill and it won't look like anything for another twenty years. No, the real change is the birds. Five years ago our annual survey recorded 92 species. This year we're already up to 118, and it's only September. Three of those had never been recorded anywhere in this county before.

A few rules before we go. Dogs are very welcome here — we're one of the few reserves that allows them — as long as they're on a lead the whole time you're on site. Bicycles are fine too, but please stay on the surfaced track, because the grass paths get churned up terribly. And the one thing we really do ask is that you don't feed the ducks and the geese. I know children love doing it, but bread does them genuine harm, it pollutes the water, and it brings in rats. There's a proper feeding station beside the visitor centre if you'd like to watch the small birds instead.

Now, a word about how all this was paid for, because we're a charity and it does matter. The visitor centre café was built with a lottery grant — a very large one; we were extremely lucky. The boardwalk over the marsh was put in by a team of volunteers from an engineering firm in town, who gave us the labour and the timber for nothing. And the extension to the car park came out of the district council's transport budget, so that cost us nothing either. But two things here were paid for entirely by donations from people living locally. The first is the new bird hide, which cost just over £40,000 and took us three years of coffee mornings and raffle tickets. The second is the pond-dipping platform, which the village primary school raised the money for almost single-handedly.

Right — let me point out where things are on the plan you've all been given.

Let's start with the wildflower meadow, because you have already walked straight past it. As you came up from the car park it was the open ground on your left, between the car park and the visitor centre. People always expect a meadow to be somewhere remote, but ours is right here at the entrance.

Now the new bird hide. Take the west path — that's the one leaving the visitor centre on your left — and follow it along the water. You'll pass a bench where the path turns north at the corner of the lake; don't stop there, keep going, and the hide is about halfway up the western shore, set back among the trees.

The pond-dipping platform is in completely the opposite direction. Come out of the centre, turn right onto the east path, and it's barely thirty metres along, right at the southern corner of the lake. You'll see the wooden railings from the door.

If you carry on north up that east path you'll come to the marsh at the top end of the lake. There's a small viewing screen about halfway along the eastern side, which people sometimes mistake for it, but the boardwalk itself crosses the marsh right at the north-eastern corner.

And finally the otter holt, which is the one that nobody ever finds. Don't look for it beside the lake at all. Go right up to the northern end, where the two paths meet — there's a signpost there — and then take the narrow track heading west along the stream. The holt is in the far north-western corner of the reserve, on the far bank. Early morning is really your only chance of seeing anything.

Right, if everybody's ready, we'll set off. Watch your footing on the first hundred metres, it's still wet from Tuesday.

sections.title: Section 3
sections.instructions: Questions 21–30. Listen to two students, Nadia and Callum, discussing their research project with their tutor, Dr Finch, and answer Questions 21–30.
sections.transcript:
DR FINCH: Come in, both of you. Right — Nadia, Callum, I've read the draft of your green roof project and there's a great deal here that's good. Shall we start with where the project has got to, and then go through the report section by section?

NADIA: Yes, please.

DR FINCH: So, the first thing I noticed is that this isn't the question you proposed back in October. You were going to compare green roofs in two different cities.

CALLUM: We were, and we did try. The problem was Kelbridge. The council there has all the temperature data — they've had monitoring equipment on eleven buildings since 2019 — but they simply wouldn't release any of it to us. We asked three times.

NADIA: In the end they told us it was commercially sensitive.

CALLUM: So we dropped the second city altogether and compared green roofs with ordinary flat roofs here in Ardwick instead.

DR FINCH: That's a sensible response. I did say at the time that two cities might be over-ambitious —

NADIA: You did, and we've thought about that since, but honestly the workload wasn't the issue. If Kelbridge had sent the figures over we'd have managed it between us.

DR FINCH: Fair enough. And you weren't worried about overlapping with Priya's group?

CALLUM: No, they're doing green walls, which turns out to be a completely different literature.

DR FINCH: Good. Now, the questionnaire. How did that go?

NADIA: Better than we expected in terms of numbers. We sent it to 200 building managers and got 84 back, which the statistics book says is more than respectable.

DR FINCH: It certainly is.

NADIA: The difficulty was the wording. Question 6 asked about annual maintenance costs, and it turned out that roughly half the people answering it thought we meant what it cost them personally, out of their own department's budget, rather than what it cost the building as a whole. So those figures aren't comparable with each other.

CALLUM: We only realised when we started coding the answers. Designing the thing took an afternoon; sorting that mess out has taken a fortnight.

DR FINCH: That's a very common problem, and the honest thing is to say so in your limitations section rather than quietly dropping the question.

CALLUM: That's what we thought.

DR FINCH: Now, the temperature measurements. Twelve buildings — is that enough, do you think?

CALLUM: We did wonder. We could probably add three or four more before Christmas.

DR FINCH: No, twelve is plenty for a project of this length, and adding buildings would only give you more of the same. And the loggers you borrowed from the department are perfectly accurate — they're calibrated every summer, so don't worry about that. My concern is when you're taking the readings. Everything in your table is from midday.

NADIA: That's when we could get access to the roofs.

DR FINCH: I understand, but midday is precisely the moment when a green roof looks its best. The interesting comparison is at dawn, and again around midnight, when the ordinary roof has lost all of its heat and the planted one hasn't. Without those you're only telling half the story.

CALLUM: The loggers can be set to record automatically overnight, can't they?

DR FINCH: They can, and they should be. So, what's next for the two of you?

NADIA: We'd said we'd go back to the Fenwick building next week and look at the drainage layer.

CALLUM: Although — hang on. We can do the Fenwick any time before the end of term; the plants aren't going anywhere. What we can't put off is Mr Okafor at the council. He's the only person who can explain the planning rules to us and he retires at the end of the month.

NADIA: Oh, that's a good point. Yes, let's do the interview next week and push the site visit back.

DR FINCH: Very sensible. Get that in the diary today, before he goes.

DR FINCH: And don't forget your presentation is on the 14th.

CALLUM: Twenty minutes, isn't it?

DR FINCH: Fifteen, plus five for questions. Handouts are optional — I know the handbook recommends one, but nobody has ever been marked down for not producing one. The rule you can't get round is that both members of the pair have to speak, and for roughly the same length of time. And it's me assessing you, not an external examiner, whatever you may have heard in the corridor.

NADIA: Right. Noted.

DR FINCH: Now, the draft itself. Your introduction: it's four and a half pages long, and about three of those repeat things you say again in the literature review. Cut it right down — two pages at the most.

CALLUM: Two pages. Right.

DR FINCH: The literature review is much better organised than your last one, I was pleased. The one weakness is that you make several claims — the one about roof lifespan, for instance — with nothing at all to support them. Go back and find the sources for those.

NADIA: We had them, we just didn't put them in.

DR FINCH: Then it's a quick job. Methodology — I wouldn't touch it. It's clear, it's honest about what went wrong, and I could repeat your study from it, which is the test. Leave it exactly as it is.

CALLUM: Good.

DR FINCH: Now, those temperature tables. There are nineteen pages of raw readings sitting in the middle of the report and they stop the reader dead. The data has to stay, obviously — but put it at the back, and keep just the summary chart in the main text.

NADIA: An appendix. Yes.

DR FINCH: And the conclusion, I'm afraid, needs starting again from nothing. At the moment it's a summary of what you did, which the reader has just finished reading. A conclusion should answer the research question and say what follows from the answer. Start with a blank page on that one.

CALLUM: Understood. That's all very clear, thank you.

DR FINCH: Send me the revised version by the 7th and I'll look at it before the presentation.

sections.title: Section 4
sections.instructions: Questions 31–40. Listen to part of a university lecture about cork and the cork oak landscape, and answer Questions 31–40.
sections.transcript:
LECTURER: Good afternoon. Today I want to look at a material that most of you handled the last time you opened a bottle, and that almost nobody ever thinks about: cork. It's a useful example of something which is both an extremely ancient product and, rather unexpectedly, a very modern one.

So, first of all, what is cork? Cork is the outer bark of a single species of tree, Quercus suber, the cork oak, which grows in the western Mediterranean — Portugal, Spain, and along the North African coast. Now, every tree has bark, but cork oak bark is unusual in two respects: it is exceptionally thick, and the tree can grow it back after it has been removed. That second property is the entire basis of the industry, and it is why cork is one of the very few forest products that does not involve felling anything.

If you put a piece of cork under a microscope, what you see is a honeycomb — millions of tiny sealed boxes, each one shaped rather like a fourteen-sided dice. The walls are made of a waxy substance called suberin, which is what makes cork waterproof, and each box is filled with a gas which is almost identical to air. And there are a great many of them: one cubic centimetre of cork contains about 40 million of these cells. That single fact explains most of cork's behaviour. It is light, because it is mostly gas. It is springy, because the gas is compressed and then pushes back. And it is a very poor conductor of both heat and sound, because the gas cannot circulate from one cell to the next.

Now, harvesting, which is where cork becomes genuinely unlike almost anything else we take out of a forest, because the tree is not cut down. It is not even damaged, provided the work is done properly.

A cork oak is left alone for a very long time. You cannot take the first harvest until the tree is 25 years old and the trunk has reached roughly seventy centimetres in circumference. After that, Portuguese law sets a minimum interval of 9 years between one stripping and the next, and in practice many estates leave it ten or even eleven.

The stripping itself is done entirely by hand, in high summer, by men who have often trained for a decade. The tool is a specially shaped axe, and no machine has ever been invented that can do the job, because the worker has to judge by sound and by feel exactly how deep to cut. Go a millimetre too deep and you damage the living layer underneath, and that tree will never produce again.

The first two harvests, incidentally, produce very poor material indeed — irregular, hard, full of cracks. It can't be made into bottle stoppers at all; it is ground up and used for things like floor tiles. It isn't until the third stripping, when the tree is well over forty years old, that you get what the trade calls reproduction cork, which is the smooth, even material a stopper is punched from. And the tree will then go on producing for two centuries. Over its whole lifetime a healthy cork oak will give about 16 harvests.

Now I want to move from the tree to the landscape, because this is the part that interests conservationists most. Cork oaks in Portugal grow in a managed system called the montado — in Spain the equivalent is called the dehesa. It looks like parkland: widely spaced oaks with grass or cereal crops growing underneath them. It is entirely man-made and has been maintained for something like a thousand years. Farmers graze pigs there, which fatten on the acorns in the autumn, and cattle and sheep on the open ground between the trees.

Ecologically the montado is remarkable. It supports up to 135 plant species per hectare, and it is the last refuge of the Iberian lynx, of which there were fewer than 100 animals left alive at the low point in 2002. Lose the montado and you lose the lynx, along with a great many birds of prey.

And the montado survives only because cork is worth money. This is really the point I want you to take away this afternoon. When the screw cap and the plastic stopper arrived in the late 1990s, natural cork lost about a third of the world wine market inside fifteen years, and in parts of southern Portugal owners simply stopped maintaining their trees. An untended montado turns into scrub within a single generation.

The industry's response has been quite interesting. Some of it is technical: the taint problem which gave cork its bad name in the first place has now largely been solved by steam treatment. But the more significant development is that cork has found markets outside the drinks trade altogether. It's used in the nose cones of spacecraft, in cricket balls, in expensive flooring and even in handbags. And the fastest-growing use of cork outside the drinks industry is building insulation — expanded cork board, which is made with no glue at all. You simply heat the granules under pressure and the suberin binds them together.

Next week we'll look at bamboo, which raises a rather different set of questions about what we mean by a sustainable material. Thank you.

sections.title: Reading Passage 1
sections.passage:
Long before mechanical refrigeration, the wealthy of several civilisations enjoyed chilled food and drink. In Persia, builders raised domed structures called yakhchals, whose thick clay walls and deep storage pits held winter ice through the desert summer. Chinese texts from the Zhou dynasty list court officials whose only duty was the filling of the royal ice cellars, and Roman authors grumbled at the price of snow carried down from the mountains to cool wine. In every one of these cases, however, ice was a luxury reserved for a small elite. What altered in the nineteenth century was not the science of keeping things cold, which changed remarkably little, but the scale on which ice could be gathered, moved and sold.

The change began with a young Bostonian named Frederic Tudor. In February 1806 he loaded ice cut from his family's pond onto the Favorite, a brig he had bought for the purpose, and sailed for the Caribbean island of Martinique, certain that the tropics would pay well for something New England discarded every spring. The voyage was a humiliation. Tudor had given almost no thought to what would happen once the cargo was landed: there was no ice house on the island, no established market for the product and no local habit of using it. Much of the cargo melted on the quayside while he searched for buyers, and he came home several thousand dollars in debt. Within a few years he had spent time in prison for money he owed.

He had, however, diagnosed the problem correctly, and he pursued it for the next forty years with a persistence that bordered on obsession. Ice, he came to understand, was not difficult to obtain; it was difficult to keep. Early cargoes were packed in hay and woollen blankets, which soaked up meltwater and rotted. The solution came from the sawmills of Maine, whose waste sawdust was almost free. Packed around the blocks, it trapped pockets of air, drained readily and did not decay, and losses on a long voyage fell from well over half the cargo to a small fraction of it. Tudor also redesigned the ice house itself, giving it double walls separated by an air gap and a raised floor that let meltwater drain away instead of pooling around the stack.

The second bottleneck was labour. Ice cut by hand with saws and chisels came out in blocks of uneven size which stacked badly, leaving air spaces through which warmth could travel. In 1825 Nathaniel Wyeth, a hotel manager who worked for Tudor, devised an ice cutter: iron blades fixed to a frame that a single horse could drag across a frozen pond, scoring the surface into a grid. The blocks prised out of that grid were square, uniform and could be packed tightly together. The cost of harvesting a tonne of ice fell by roughly nine-tenths, and one man with a horse did the work of a dozen with saws.

Supply was useless without demand, and Tudor's third innovation was commercial rather than technical. On reaching a new port he would give ice away to bar keepers and cafe owners on condition that they used it for a whole season. Customers who had grown accustomed to a cold drink would not willingly go back to a warm one, and when the free supply ended the merchants had little choice but to buy. Any rival who appeared was undercut, sometimes at a loss, until he withdrew.

The trade's most improbable success came in 1833, when the Tuscany sailed from Boston to Calcutta carrying about 180 tonnes of ice. The voyage crossed the equator twice and lasted four months. Roughly two-thirds of the cargo survived the journey, and the profits were such that the merchants of Calcutta raised a subscription and built a substantial store to receive future shipments. For much of the century, ice cut from ponds within a day's cart ride of Boston was on sale in India, Cuba, Brazil and the Philippines.

In Britain the product acquired something close to a brand name. Ice from Wenham Lake, north of Boston, was thought unusually clear, and from 1845 the Wenham Lake Ice Company kept premises in the Strand in London, where a block was displayed in the window each morning with a newspaper placed behind it so that passers-by could read through the ice. The name became a byword for quality, so much so that Norwegian exporters later renamed a lake near Oslo in order to sell their own ice under it.

The end came from two directions at once. From the 1870s onwards, machines that made ice by compressing and expanding ammonia became reliable and cheap enough to install in breweries, meat works and eventually ordinary shops, and they worked just as well in a warm winter as in a cold one. At the same time the natural product began to lose its reputation. Ponds and rivers near expanding cities were receiving untreated sewage, and public health officials linked contaminated ice to outbreaks of typhoid. A commodity whose chief virtue was purity could not long survive the suspicion that it carried disease. By 1920 the natural ice trade of North America had all but disappeared, though the insulated stores and delivery rounds it had created were inherited, almost unchanged, by the manufacturers who replaced it.

sections.title: Reading Passage 2
sections.passage:
A Few forests are as easy to recognise, or as hard to love at first sight, as a mangrove. Seen from a boat at low tide, a mangrove stand is a thicket of glossy leaves balanced on a tangle of pale roots above grey, sulphurous mud. Yet the word mangrove does not describe a family of plants at all. It is an ecological label rather than a taxonomic one: some seventy species drawn from more than twenty unrelated plant families have independently arrived at the same way of life, growing in the intertidal zone of tropical and subtropical coasts where fresh water meets salt and where the ground is flooded and drained twice a day. What such plants share is not ancestry but circumstance.

B The conditions they tolerate would kill almost any other tree. Seawater draws moisture out of ordinary root cells rather than supplying it, and mangroves meet this difficulty in two ways: an ultrafiltration membrane at the root surface excludes as much as nine-tenths of the salt in the water they take up, and glands in the leaves of some species excrete whatever gets through, leaving visible crystals on the surface. The mud poses a second problem, since waterlogged sediment holds almost no oxygen. Many mangroves therefore produce pneumatophores, pencil-shaped aerial roots that grow vertically out of the mud and admit air through pores when the tide is out. A third adaptation concerns reproduction. A seed dropped into moving salt water has little chance of finding anywhere to germinate, so many mangroves are viviparous: the seed sprouts while still attached to the parent, and what eventually drops is not a seed but a propagule, a ready-made seedling that may drift for weeks before lodging in soft mud and putting out roots within hours.

C That root tangle, so awkward for anyone on foot, is the reason coastal fishing communities have always valued mangroves. The submerged prop roots create a maze of shaded, structurally complex water in which small animals can hide from larger ones, and a great many commercially important fish, crabs and prawns pass part of their life cycle there before moving out to open water or reef. Where mangroves have been cleared, catches of these species have generally fallen, and one widely cited set of estimates puts the annual value of a hectare of intact mangrove to nearby fisheries well above the return from most of the uses for which mangroves are cleared. That benefit, however, is spread thinly across many small operators rather than concentrated in a single owner, and so rarely appears on anybody's balance sheet.

D The belief that mangroves shield the coast behind them is older than the evidence for it. After the Indian Ocean tsunami of December 2004, several rapid studies reported that villages standing behind wide belts of mangrove had suffered far fewer deaths than comparable villages on cleared shorelines. The more careful analyses that followed were considerably cooler. Some of the sheltered villages, it emerged, also lay behind sand ridges, or further from the water, or at greater elevation, and the statistical methods used could not separate the trees from the terrain. The position that has settled out of the argument is narrower but much better supported: against a wave of that size a belt of trees offers only limited protection, but against the ordinary, incessant forces that shape coastlines - wind-driven waves, storm surge and the erosion of the shore itself - mangroves are demonstrably effective.

E The most recent argument for mangroves is one that nobody made at all until the present century. Hectare for hectare, mangrove forests lock away carbon several times faster than most tropical rainforest, and the greater part of the store - commonly more than two-thirds of it - is not in the wood above the water but in the sediment underneath. Waterlogged mud contains so little oxygen that the bacteria which normally break down dead plant material work extremely slowly, and organic matter simply accumulates for millennia. The implication is uncomfortable for anyone clearing a mangrove: felling the trees releases a few decades of growth, but draining and digging out the sediment releases the accumulation of millennia.

F That is very largely what happened over the late twentieth century. Between 1980 and 2000 the world lost something in the region of a quarter of its mangroves, an unusually rapid decline for any forest type. Ponds for farmed prawns were the single largest cause across South-East Asia and Latin America, followed by rice paddy, salt pans, timber and charcoal cutting, and the ordinary spread of ports, roads and housing along a shoreline. Mangroves were an easy target: they stood on ground that few people owned outright, they were widely regarded as wasteland, and in several countries the law classified them as exactly that. Since 2000 the rate of loss has slowed markedly, partly because much of the accessible forest had already gone and partly because a number of governments began to protect what remained.

G Protection has been accompanied by a great deal of replanting, and here the record is poor. Governments, aid agencies and companies have put many millions of seedlings into the ground, usually with volunteers and a photographer present, and follow-up surveys in the Philippines, Sri Lanka and elsewhere have repeatedly found survival rates below one-fifth after a few years. The commonest mistake is not botanical but geographical. Planters favour the genus Rhizophora because its long, heavy propagules are easy to collect, easy to carry and easy to push into soft ground; and they plant them on open mudflats and seagrass beds low in the tidal frame, because such places are empty and nobody objects. But mangroves do not naturally grow there. They grow higher up the shore, where the tide covers the ground for only part of the day, and a seedling planted below that zone is drowned by degrees.

H The alternative approach, usually called ecological mangrove restoration, starts from the observation that mangroves are good at colonising suitable ground without any help; if they are absent from a place where they once grew, something is preventing them from returning. Its practitioners therefore begin by studying the movement of water across a degraded site and identifying the obstruction, most often the wall of an abandoned prawn pond or a road embankment that has cut the site off from the tide. Removing the barrier and restoring the flow will, at many sites, bring the forest back unaided within a few years, and with a mixture of species that no planting scheme would have chosen. Seedlings are used only where there is no source of propagules nearby. The remaining difficulty is not ecological but social: a degraded pond belongs to somebody, or is claimed by several people at once, and until the question of who holds the land has been settled, the hydrology will stay exactly as it is.

sections.title: Reading Passage 3
sections.passage:
Anyone who wants to argue that schools should not be measured has a weak hand, and I do not intend to play it. Public education consumes an enormous share of public money and shapes the prospects of every child who passes through it; the idea that its results should be taken on trust is indefensible. The argument I want to make is narrower, and I think more serious. It is that the way we now measure schooling has stopped being a description of what schools do and has become the thing that schools do - and that a measure which behaves in this way tells us progressively less about the very quality it was designed to capture.

The case for measurement is easily stated and largely correct. External written examinations, when they were first introduced, broke the grip of patronage on entry to universities and the professions: a candidate's paper could be marked without anyone knowing whose son he was. More recently, published results have made certain kinds of failure impossible to deny. Before national data were collected, a school could serve a poor neighbourhood badly for a generation while describing itself as doing its best in difficult circumstances, and nobody outside the building could prove otherwise. The numbers ended that particular comfort, and any reform that quietly restored it would be a reform in the wrong direction. Injustice that cannot be counted is injustice that is easily denied.

The difficulty appears at the next step, when a number collected in order to observe a system is used instead to steer it. Economists have a name for what follows. Goodhart's law, formulated in the 1970s in relation to monetary policy, holds that when a measure becomes a target it ceases to be a good measure - not because those affected are dishonest, but because any indicator is only a partial proxy for the thing it stands for, and pressure applied to the proxy travels first into the gap between the two. A school judged on the proportion of its pupils reaching a particular grade will improve that proportion. Whether it has improved education is a separate question, and one the indicator is no longer able to answer.

Consider first what happens to the timetable. Where results in two or three subjects determine a school's public standing, its funding and, in some systems, the employment of its head teacher, hours drift towards those subjects and away from everything else. Surveys of primary teachers in England and in the United States have described the same pattern: less time for history, geography, art and music, and, in the weeks before a test, a curriculum consisting largely of past papers, question formats and the particular habits of the marking scheme. This is not cheating, and the teachers involved are not cynics. They are responding, sensibly, to the only signal the system sends them clearly.

Consider next what happens to pupils. If a school is judged on the number of children who cross a threshold, the children who matter to that number are the ones already close to it. Extra tuition, the strongest teachers and the head teacher's attention flow towards the borderline; pupils comfortably above it, and those far enough below it that no plausible effort will carry them across in time, are of no consequence to the published figure. Researchers have called this educational triage, and it is not the fault of the schools that practise it. The system asks them to move a certain number of children across a line, and they do exactly that, which is precisely the problem.

Does any of this actually distort the results themselves? The evidence says that it does. One American researcher has spent much of his career comparing scores on high-stakes tests with those from independent, low-stakes surveys sat by the same pupils in the same subjects. The pattern is consistent: where results on the high-stakes test have risen steeply, the low-stakes measure shows a small improvement or none at all. The gain, in other words, lies largely in the test rather than in the pupils. It is inflation, and, as with the monetary kind, the figures go on looking excellent for exactly as long as nobody asks what they now buy.

There is a deeper problem behind that one. Tests measure what is cheap and quick to measure, and what is cheap to measure is not what education is chiefly for. A marker can establish rapidly whether a pupil recalls the date of a treaty or applies a familiar procedure to a familiar equation. It is far harder to establish whether she can hold an argument together over four pages, work usefully with people she did not choose, or keep going at a problem that refuses to yield in twenty minutes. Qualities such as perseverance are therefore barely touched by the instruments we rely on, and - this is the part that should worry us - in a system driven by measurement, a quality that goes unmeasured is a quality that quietly stops being taught. Not everything that counts can be counted, runs the remark usually attributed to Einstein; it was in fact written by a sociologist, William Bruce Cameron, some years after Einstein's death, which is itself a modest illustration of how loosely we handle evidence when a phrase is convenient.

The remedy is not to stop measuring. It is to change how much rests on the measurement. A country can find out how well its children read by testing a carefully drawn sample of them, as several already do, rather than every child in every school every year; the resulting figures are more than accurate enough to guide policy, and no individual school's fate hangs on them. Judgements about a particular school can then be made in the way we make judgements about a hospital or a court - by people who understand the work, who visit, who look at what pupils have actually produced across a year, and whose assessments are moderated against those of colleagues elsewhere in order to keep them honest. Such arrangements are slower and messier than a league table, and they demand something a league table does not: a willingness to trust professionals whom one has also taken the trouble to inspect.

None of this is an argument for ignorance. It is an argument about what we do with knowledge once we have it. A thermometer held over a candle will show a rising temperature, and if we have agreed in advance to reward whoever produces the highest reading, we shall end up with a great many candles and a room that is no warmer than before.

questions.prompt:
The bar chart below shows the percentage of commuters in the European city of Riverton who travelled to work by four different means of transport in 2000 and in 2020.

Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

Write at least 150 words.
questions.sampleAnswer:
The bar chart compares the proportions of commuters in the European city of Riverton who used four different means of transport to get to work in 2000 and 2020.

Overall, the private car remained the most popular option throughout the period, although its share fell substantially. Meanwhile, the two modes that gained ground were the train and the bicycle, the latter of which recorded the sharpest relative increase.

In 2000, over half of all commuters, at 55%, drove to work, more than twice the figure for the next most common mode, the bus, at 22%. Rail travel accounted for 13% of journeys, while just one commuter in ten cycled.

Twenty years later, the picture had become considerably more balanced. Car use had dropped by 17 percentage points to 38%, and although driving was still the leading choice, its dominance was much less pronounced. Train use, by contrast, had doubled to 26%, overtaking the bus to become the second most popular option. Cycling also grew markedly, from 10% to 18%, while the bus was the only other mode to decline, slipping modestly to the same 18% share.

questions.prompt:
Some people believe that all secondary school students should be required to complete a period of unpaid work in their local community before they are allowed to graduate.

To what extent do you agree or disagree?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

Write at least 250 words.
questions.sampleAnswer:
It has been suggested that no student should leave secondary school without first having spent time volunteering in their local area. I largely agree with this proposal, provided that the placements are properly designed and do not degenerate into a box-ticking exercise.

The strongest argument in favour of compulsory community service is that it teaches lessons which cannot be delivered in a classroom. Adolescents who spend a term helping in a food bank, a care home or a primary school are confronted at first hand with the realities of poverty, ageing and disadvantage, and this tends to produce a degree of empathy and civic awareness that no textbook can generate. In Germany, where a voluntary social year has long been an established route for school leavers, participants consistently report that the experience shaped both their values and their eventual choice of career.

A second benefit is more practical. Employers routinely complain that young applicants lack the so-called soft skills of punctuality, teamwork and communication, and a placement outside the sheltered environment of school is an inexpensive way of developing them. A seventeen-year-old who has had to organise a weekly activity session for elderly residents has learned to plan, negotiate and take responsibility in a way that written examinations simply do not test.

The obvious objection is that compulsion sits awkwardly with the spirit of volunteering, and that already overloaded students may come to resent a further demand on their time. This is a fair concern, but it is an argument for careful implementation rather than for abandoning the idea altogether: a modest requirement of, say, forty hours spread across two years, combined with a genuine choice of placement, would keep the burden manageable.

In conclusion, while such a scheme must be sensitively managed, I believe the social and personal benefits of requiring community service clearly outweigh the reservations about making it obligatory.
